summary:
This is a short survey (IJCAI-22 Survey Track) of text-only multi-party conversation (MPC) research. It frames MPC as a (speaker, utterance, addressee) triple: "Who says What to Whom". In a two-party chat, messages alternate in a line. In MPC the structure is a graph: any speaker can address anyone, and several replies can answer the same earlier message (Fig. 1).

Figure 2's taxonomy has two branches.
(A) Conversational context modeling:
- discourse parsing (reply-to relations such as clarification, answer, acknowledgement, elaboration; STAC corpus)
- information flow (sequential vs graphical: homogeneous graphs like GSN, heterogeneous graphs like HeterMPC and TUCORE-GCN)
- self-supervision (pre-training such as MPC-BERT, and auxiliary tasks such as topic prediction/disentanglement and speaker prediction)

(B) Conversational component modeling:
- WHO speaks: utterance-unaware turn-taking (predict the next speaker from history only) vs utterance-aware speaker identification
- say WHAT: retrieval-based vs generation-based responses
- address WHOM: explicit addressee recognition vs implicit addressing via dialogue disentanglement / thread detection

It closes with four open challenges: universal MPC understanding (joint tasks plus dynamic topic and structure tracking), modeling heterogeneity, high-level MPC applications, and low- or zero-resource MPC.

Gaps that matter for us: nothing on voice or speech, latency, barge-in, or when to stay silent. The closest it gets is one sentence in the introduction saying it matters to know "when an agent must wait before interacting". Its one deployed multi-bot system (finch) runs turn-taking with a rule-based finite-state automaton (FSA).
findings: §1 Intro: the paper names our setting directly: 'multiple people may want to interact with a chatbot or one person interacts with several chatbots at the same time, as in a chat group'. It says the core abilities are (1) predicting 'which agent in the conversation is the most likely to speak next, and conversely, when an agent must wait before interacting', (2) detecting who is being addressed, and (3) responding only 'after knowing a speaker and an addressee at the current dialogue state'. So the field orders the decision as who speaks → to whom → what. Jev's job is the first two.

§1 / Fig. 1: MPC information flow is a graph, not a sequence. U3 and U4 both reply to U2, and U5 and U6 both reply to U3. A router that reads the room as a flat, ordered transcript (Fig. 2 'Sequential Flow') 'fall[s] short in modeling complicated reply-to relationships' (§2.2).

§2.1 Discourse parsing: a follow-up utterance can be 'a clarification or an answer of a question raised in the conversation history, or an acknowledgement or an elaboration'. Typing the reply-to relation is exactly what our known gap needs: recognising that a human's later message is an 'answer' to the question that triggered dispatch. Wang et al. 2021 (edge-centric GNN, no reliance on its own earlier predictions, to avoid error propagation) is the stated SOTA.

§2.2: heterogeneous graphs of utterance and interlocutor nodes with type-dependent parameters beat utterance-only graphs (Gu et al., HeterMPC). Lee & Choi's dialogue graph has four node types and three edge types, and the survey calls it SOTA on MPC graph representation. In a design reading: Jev's context should carry WHO said each line and WHOM it replied to, not just the text.

§2.3 Auxiliary training: Wang et al. 2020 add topic prediction and topic disentanglement so models can track parallel topics. Li & Zhao add self-supervised speaker prediction plus key-utterance prediction 'to capture salient utterances in a long and noisy dialogue'.

§3.1 WHO speaks, utterance-unaware turn-taking: predict s_n given {(s1,u1)…(s_{n-1},u_{n-1})}. This means 'modeling the coordination strategies that speakers adopt to acquire or give up the floor'. finch (Pinhanez et al.; de Bayser et al. 2018) has 'one person and four collaborative chatbots which are experts in financial investments', and its turn-taking 'is controlled by a rule-based Finite-State Automata (FSA) service ... called for every utterance ... considering both conversation history and interactions between interlocutors'. de Bayser 2019 compares MLE, SVM, CNN and LSTM for next-speaker prediction. Hawes et al.: CRFs on Supreme Court transcripts. This is the closest prior art to Jev plus our deterministic rules, and it supports a hybrid of rules plus a learned or LLM picker.

§3.1 utterance-aware: 'who will be the next speaker in an MPC could have multiple answers since multiple sub-conversation threads are assumed to occur simultaneously'. A single-responder choice is a simplification that holds per thread, not per room. Our one-responder rule can be wrong when two unrelated threads interleave.

§3.1 speaker segmentation (Meng 2017): a speaker change is detected as binary classification over utterance pairs. Speaker searching (Gu et al., MPC-BERT) is the stated SOTA for speaker identification.

§3.2 Say WHAT: for DSTC8, 'a full excerpt is composed of hundreds of utterances', so it is 'necessary to pre-filter these utterances'. The top-three DSTC8 teams 'all design various heuristic rules to extract addressee- and speaker-related features for context disentanglement'. Wang et al. treat response selection as dynamic topic tracking ('topic should remain the same as going from contexts to responses'). Implication: the context sent to Jev should be filtered by thread and addressee, not just the most recent N messages.

§3.3 Explicit addressee recognition: 'the explicit declaration of names of addressees is more common in text-only-based conversations' than face-to-face. This supports our name-opens-message = mention rule for chat, and implies spoken or voice addressing will be more implicit. Zhang et al. (2018) give three per-turn roles: 'sender, addressee, observer'. Roles 'vary across turns', and interlocutor embeddings are updated 'role-sensitively'. Our active/mentions/observe listen modes are static per member, while the literature's roles are per turn. Le et al. (W2W) recover addressees for every utterance, including unspecified ones, and MPC-BERT is SOTA here.

§3.3 Implicit addressing, i.e. disentanglement: 'most of the existing methods are designed to find out which previous utterance in the history the current utterance is replying to. Thus, this task is in essence modeling addressees implicitly.' Useful features (Kummerfeld 2019): 'time, directedness, word overlap, and context'. Pappadopulo et al. use 'user turns and mentions'. Yu & Joty treat it as pointing: a pointer network producing a multinomial distribution over previous utterances (SOTA). Liu et al. 2020 do online, transition-based disentanglement, adding each utterance to its best-matching session, which is the streaming setting we are in.

§4 Open challenges: an MPC system 'should be able to track topic transitions and update the conversation structure dynamically as a conversation proceeds'. Also: 'a shared topic tracker at a coarse granularity cannot understand in-depth', so track sub-conversations at fine granularity. Other challenges: heterogeneous graphs, cross-domain high-level understanding, and low- or zero-resource MPC (not yet explored for MPC).

What is absent (useful negatives): no treatment of speech, overlapping talk, latency, barge-in, wake words or floor control in audio. Nothing on whether an agent should stay silent beyond the one intro sentence. Nothing on revoking a decision after newer messages arrive. No calibration or confidence thresholds. The survey is text-only by its own scope ('text-based MPCs'), so none of Jev's voice rules or its 0.7 silence threshold can be checked against it.

forLightbulb:
1) Jev is solving the survey's 'WHO speaks' problem, and the closest prior art agrees with our shape: finch used a rule-based finite-state automaton for one human and four expert bots, called on every utterance. That supports keeping our deterministic rules (name = mention, addressed is not ambient, the agent-hop cap) as a rule layer in front of the LLM. It does not validate the 0.7 threshold or the silence-by-default rule. The paper has no evidence on either.

2) The paper's central structural claim is that MPC is a reply graph, not a sequence, and that several threads run at once. Jev should see each line's author and reply-to edge, and per-turn roles (sender, addressee, observer), not a flat transcript. Our static per-room listen modes are a coarse version of Zhang et al.'s per-turn roles. 'One responder per message' assumes a single thread. When threads interleave, the right answer can be one responder per thread.

3) The known gap (Jev decides at dispatch and misses a human answering seconds later) is the field's 'answer' reply-to relation (§2.1) plus online disentanglement (§3.3, Liu et al. 2020). The survey's open challenge says to 'update the conversation structure dynamically as a conversation proceeds'. Concretely: before an agent posts, recheck whether any newer human message links back (reply-to, typed 'answer') to the triggering question, and if so drop the post or convert it to an ack. Cheap features the literature uses for linking: time gap, directedness (@ or name), word overlap, same speaker pair.

4) Addressee naming is 'more common in text-only' conversations. Expect weaker explicit naming in Live voice, so the wake name and floor-holder rules carry more of the load there, and recall on implicit addressing will be worse than in chat.

5) DSTC8 winners pre-filtered long histories by addressee and speaker heuristics. Feeding Jev a thread-filtered context, rather than the last N messages, is the indicated direction for busy rooms.

6) There is nothing here to borrow for voice barge-in, queueing or stop. Look elsewhere (spoken-dialogue turn-taking literature) for those.
testIdeas: Answered-before-dispatch race: Alice asks 'what's our MRR?' (no agent named, Finance active). Within 3 s Bob replies 'it's $12k, just checked Stripe'. Expected: Finance does not post an answer. At most it adds a short confirmation if its number differs. This tests the reply-to 'answer' relation and the recheck before posting.

Interleaved threads (Fig. 1 shape): Alice and Bob discuss a launch date while Carol, in the same room, asks 'can someone pull last week's churn?'. Expected: Analytics answers Carol, and no agent replies to the launch thread unless addressed. Two threads can each have at most one responder; Carol's ask is not suppressed because the room is busy.

Implicit addressee via reply-to: Engineering posts a question to Alice. Alice replies 'yes, go ahead' without naming anyone. Expected: only Engineering acts, and the CEO and others stay silent. This is implicit addressee recovery through the reply-to link to the previous speaker.

Per-turn role shift: Alice @mentions Growth. Two messages later, Growth's message mentions Finance's numbers and Alice says 'Finance, confirm?'. Expected: Finance speaks (now the addressee) and Growth does not reply again (now an observer this turn).

Person-addressed then ambient: 'Prasiddha, can you approve the budget?' followed 20 s later by 'anyone know the vendor's terms?' with no name. Expected: the first gets silence from all agents (opens with a person's name), and the second is eligible for one active agent. Silence must not carry over to the next unaddressed message.

Agent-to-agent chain with the human mid-thread: Engineering posts a question to Finance (agent message; silence unless confidence ≥0.7). The human then answers it before Finance's run starts. Expected: Finance does not post a duplicate answer, and the hop cap is not hit.

Voice, implicit addressing: in Live, Alice says 'what do you think?' right after the CEO finished speaking, with no wake name. Expected: the CEO answers, because it was the previous speaker and the likely addressee. Other agents do not barge in. Contrast with the same line after a human spoke: nobody answers.

Voice, human answers mid-queue: Alice asks a question, Finance is queued for the floor, and Bob answers aloud first. Expected: Finance's queued turn is dropped or turned into a brief 'agree', not a full repeat. This is the voice analogue of the dispatch race.

Long noisy history: 200 messages of off-topic chatter, then 'Ops, did the refund go out for order 1182?'. Expected: Customer Operations answers using the refund thread from 150 messages earlier. This tests thread-filtered context over a last-N window (the DSTC8 pre-filter lesson).

summary:
GIFT is a fine-tuning method for Transformer encoders (BERT, SA-BERT, MPC-BERT) on multi-party conversation (MPC) understanding. The context is the whole conversation, concatenated with a [CLS] token before each utterance and speaker embeddings added (§3.2). Every token-pair attention logit is scaled by one learned scalar per edge type, chosen by how the two utterances relate: reply-to, replied-by, reply-self, or indirect-reply (everything else) (§3.3, Eq. 3). That adds 4 parameters per layer. The reply edges come from gold addressee labels on the history utterances; the last utterance's own reply-to edge is masked.

They test three tasks, each predicting something about the LAST utterance only:
- Addressee recognition: pick the preceding utterance whose speaker is the addressee (Eq. 4–5).
- Speaker identification: find utterances with the same speaker, with the last speaker's embedding masked.
- Response selection: binary matching of context and candidate response (Eq. 6–7).

Data is Ubuntu IRC only: Hu et al. 2019, and Ouchi & Tsuboi 2016 split into Len-5/10/15. GIFT improves every base model on every task and set. Speaker identification gains the most (+7 to +29 points P@1). Addressee recognition gains up to +5.75 and response selection up to +5.35 R10@1.

Ablations (Table 5): removing the reply-to/replied-by distinction costs the most. Merging the two directions costs some, and so does merging reply-self into indirect.

Length analysis (Fig. 3, Table 6): addressee and speaker accuracy fall as sessions get longer for every model, and GIFT models fall less in 14 of 18 cases.

The authors' stated limitations: the method depends on addressee labels for the history ("an MPC with a few addressee labels missing is a common issue", left as future work), it needs full attention (latency cost when deployed), and it was evaluated only on Ubuntu IRC.

The paper does not model whether anyone should respond. Every task assumes the last utterance has an addressee among the participants, so there is no "none" class. It has no timing, no turn-taking or floor, no voice, and no case of a human answering before the system does.
findings: §3.3 / Eq. 3: Atten(q,k,v) = softmax(φ(e_q,v) · qᵀk/√d) v, where e ∈ {reply-to, replied-by, reply-self, indirect-reply}. The edge type between two utterances is applied to every token in them. 'Lightweight' means 4 scalars per encoding layer.

§3.3 gives each edge a meaning. Reply-to models what the current utterance should look like given the one it replies to. Replied-by models how later utterances change the reading of the current one. Reply-self controls how much of the original meaning is kept. Indirect-reply covers the rest of the context.

§4.1 and footnote 1: they predict only the LAST utterance's addressee, because the history's reply labels are the graph input and evaluating those would leak. In deployment terms, the structure of past messages is treated as known and only the newest message is inferred.

§4.1: addressee recognition is reframed as 'which preceding utterance's speaker is the addressee'. The answer space is the people who already spoke in the context. Nobody absent can be chosen, and 'no one' cannot be chosen.

Appendix A.1 baseline 'Preceding' (Le et al. 2019): the addressee is the speaker who spoke just before the current speaker. It scores 55.73 / 55.63 / 55.62 P@1 (Table 2), against 83.61–85.85 for MPC-BERT w/ GIFT. A last-speaker heuristic gets roughly half the hard cases wrong.

Table 2 (addressee recognition) and Fig. 3a / Table 6: accuracy drops as conversations get longer. MPC-BERT goes 84.21 → 80.67 → 78.98. GIFT narrows the drop (85.85 → 84.13 → 83.61) but does not remove it.

Table 3 (speaker identification): GIFT's biggest gains are here. BERT goes 62.24 → 89.74 on Len-5. The authors say the method is 'particularly useful for speaker identification'. Who-said-what structure is what flat sequence encoders lose the most.

Table 5 ablation (validation set of Hu et al. 2019): merging reply-to and replied-by into indirect drops speaker identification sharply (BERT 86.50 → 70.67; MPC-BERT 91.72 → 84.32). Collapsing the two directions into one costs less (BERT SI 85.67). Merging reply-self costs a little (BERT RS 75.26 → 74.72). The direction of a reply edge carries information.

§5.5 / Fig. 4: indirect-reply weights start lowest and end highest in the last layer (0.9834 vs 0.9825 reply-to and 0.9821 replied-by, layer 12, Fig. 4c). The authors read this as attending to the directly related turns first and to the wider context afterwards.
§5.4 response selection: GIFT adds +0.88 to +5.35 R10@1. MPC-BERT on Hu et al. R2@1 (94.90 → 95.04) and on Len-5 R2@1 (87.63 → 87.97) are not marked significant.

Limitations section: it needs full attention across all utterances, so 'computational complexity and inference latency may be worth considering' online. It was evaluated only on the domain-specific Ubuntu IRC data. The Conclusion adds that it depends on addressee labels, and missing labels are common.

Not in the paper: deciding to stay silent, a 'no addressee' or 'not for any agent' class, more than one candidate system speaker, timing or race conditions, voice turn-taking, or humans answering before the system.

Minor: the ACL checklist cites 'Appendix A.1' for data statistics and 'Appendix A.3' for compute and hyperparameters. A.3 does not exist (the appendices are A, A.1, A.2, B). The statistics are in Table 1 and the hyperparameters in §5.3.

forLightbulb:
1. Give Jev an explicit reply graph, not a flat transcript. The paper's core result is that a strong encoder reading a concatenated chat underuses who-replied-to-whom structure, and adding even 4 scalars of edge type helps. Speaker identification goes from about 62 to 90 P@1 on Len-5 (Table 3). Jev is a prompted LLM, not fine-tuned, so the equivalent change is serialising each prior message as (speaker, kind=human|agent, addressee/replyTo, threadParent, isSelf-for-candidate) instead of 'Name: text'. We already have most of the edges as data: @mentions, the opening-name rule, thread parents, triggerMessageId and agentHop. Reply-self maps to marking, for each candidate agent, which messages are its own. The ablation says to keep direction: show 'X replied to Y', not just 'X and Y talked'.

2. Our deterministic fallback is the paper's 'Preceding' baseline, and it is weak. The fallback for a human message when Jev is down ('candidate who last spoke in that thread, else in the room, else CEO') is close to Le et al.'s Preceding heuristic, about 55.7% P@1 on Ubuntu IRC (Table 2). That supports the current silence-on-outage rules for agent-authored and person-addressed messages. It argues against widening the fallback, and for logging fallback picks so we can measure how often they were wrong.

3. Long context hurts addressee recognition for everyone (Table 2, Fig. 3a, Table 6). Jev should get a bounded, structure-annotated window centred on the message's thread and the candidates' recent turns, not an ever-growing room history. If we have to trim, keep the reply edges and drop the indirect context first.

4. The paper does not cover our hardest decisions:
- There is no 'none' class. Its addressee is always a prior speaker, so the paper gives no evidence for the 0.7 silence threshold.
- It has no timing. Like Jev today, it predicts from history that is already complete.
- It has no voice floor, queue or barge-in.

Our known gap is that Jev decides at dispatch and cannot see a human answer seconds later. The paper's framing suggests one fix: the replied-by edge says later turns revise how an earlier one should be read. Re-check before posting: the agent, or a cheap Jev re-check at reply time, re-reads messages that arrived after the trigger. If any of them replies to the trigger (a thread reply, a quote, or the next human message from someone other than the asker), the agent drops or folds its answer.

5. A training-data or eval hint: the authors flag missing addressee labels as the open problem. Our rooms carry explicit addressee signals (mentions, DMs, threads, voice wake names), so we can build a labelled eval set from production decisions cheaply. Ubuntu IRC results may not transfer to mixed human/agent business rooms; the paper itself warns about domain.

summary:
This is a short EMNLP 2024 diagnostic study (FBK, Trento) of how well an LLM understands multi-party chat. It uses Llama2-13b-chat, zero-shot, with no fine-tuning. Candidates are scored by conditional perplexity: the model never generates an answer; the candidate it finds least surprising wins.

There are two tasks, and in both the next speaker is GIVEN:
- Response Selection (RS): pick the real next message out of two candidates (chance 0.5).
- Addressee Recognition (AR): predict whom the next message is addressed to. The choices are every participant so far plus a dummy [OTHER] user who never appeared, so there are 4 to 7 choices and chance is 0.25 to 0.14.

Data is the Ubuntu IRC corpus, cut to 15 messages per conversation and split into four "diagnostic" subsets with exactly 3, 4, 5 and 6 users (1200, 635, 520 and 350 conversations). Usernames are replaced with gender-neutral tags, and [ALEX] is always the next speaker.

The conversation can be given to the model in four forms:
- Conversation transcript (CONV): speaker plus text.
- Interaction transcript (STRUCT): speaker to addressee only, no text.
- A summary written by the LLM (three topics).
- A description of the next speaker written by the LLM (five adjectives).

These are combined six ways, each under three prompt styles (verbose, medium, concise).

Main results:
1. AR depends on structure. The who-talked-to-whom list alone does about as well as list plus text, and text alone is worst.
2. RS depends on text. Structure adds nothing.
3. AR is far more sensitive to prompt wording than RS, and the verbose prompt usually wins for AR.
4. The key diagnostic: AR accuracy falls as the next speaker's degree centrality rises, meaning the more distinct people they have talked to. The structure advantage holds mainly when the speaker has talked to only one or two people. Past that, every input format converges and drops.
5. Summaries come close to the best result only in the hardest settings (6 users, high centrality). The speaker descriptions are mostly useless.

The authors themselves say: one dataset, one model, best-run reporting, and the results should not be taken as general model capability.
findings: Task framing (Sec 3): in both tasks the identity of the NEXT SPEAKER IS GIVEN. Neither task asks 'who should speak next' or 'should anyone speak'. So the paper does not measure Jev's actual decision (pick the responder or none). It measures a neighbouring skill: knowing who is talking to whom.

Method (Sec 4.2, App B.2): no answer is generated. Each candidate is scored by conditional perplexity, CPPL(r|p) = 1/P(r|p)^(1/|r|), the lowest wins, and normalised 1/CPPL gives a probability per candidate. The authors report that correlating that probability with the network metrics gives the same conclusions as accuracy.

Input formats (Sec 4.1): CONV is the ordered speaker and text list. STRUCT is the ordered 'speaker to addressee' list with no text. SUMM is three topics with explanations from the next speaker's perspective. DESC is five adjectives describing the next speaker. All are generated by the same Llama2-13b-chat with greedy decoding.
Six combinations (Sec 6): CONV, CONV+STRUCT, STRUCT+SUMM, STRUCT+DESC, STRUCT+SUMM+DESC, and STRUCT alone (AR only, since STRUCT has no text for RS).

AR macro result (Sec 7, Fig 5, Table 2): CONV+STRUCT and STRUCT alone are consistently best on every dataset, and text-only CONV is consistently worst. SUMM beats DESC on every dataset. CONV+STRUCT still beats both of them.

RS macro result (Sec 7, Table 3): CONV and CONV+STRUCT are best everywhere. Among the summary and description inputs, STRUCT+SUMM+DESC is best on Ubuntu3/4 and STRUCT+SUMM on Ubuntu5/6. STRUCT+DESC is worst for both tasks everywhere, except AR on Ubuntu3.

Prompt sensitivity (Sec 7, Table 1): relative gap = 1 - average/best across the three prompt styles. It is far larger for AR than for RS on every dataset. The verbose prompt is the best one for AR in most settings (marked with a diamond in Table 1); RS shows no consistent benefit from verbosity. In the Discussion (Sec 8) the authors guess why: RS resembles the next-token pretraining task.

Structural diagnosis (Sec 7, Fig 6): for AR, degree centrality deg(u) of the next speaker (how many distinct users they have interacted with) shows the strongest correlation with accuracy: 'higher deg(u) values consistently correspond to lower accuracy'. The gap between the best inputs (CONV+STRUCT, STRUCT) and the rest is widest when deg(u) is low. STRUCT 'is highly effective when the next speaker has spoken with few users in the transcripts (one or two), but it performs like the other combinations when the next speaker spoke with more than two users.'

Average outgoing weight (messages per partner, Sec 5.1, 7, 8): weaker correlation. Higher weight goes with somewhat higher AR accuracy for the STRUCT-based inputs. The authors note this may just be the flip side of low degree, since the length is fixed at 15.
RS shows no clear correlation with either network metric (Sec 7, 8). Either the structure does not matter for picking a response, or the model infers the flow from the text alone.

Macro scores hide this (Sec 8 RQ3): 'the best input combinations perform very well in simpler conversations, with limited generalization to more complex interaction structures'. A capable model should degrade less as degree centrality grows.

Compression (Sec 8): the gap between the best input and the best summary-based input shrinks as more users are involved, so summaries may be viable for large groups. 'Overall, user descriptions appear to be ineffective.' The authors partly blame bad summaries from Llama2-13b.
Closeness centrality and clustering coefficient were also tested. Both correlated strongly with degree centrality, so they are not reported (Sec 8).

Appendix A: the prompt is built from seven fixed sections (scenario, input elements, task definition, user space, input format, instruction template, output template). The [OTHER] option means 'addressing a speaker not in the conversation'. A second output template for the summary and description changed results by at most 1.9% (App B.4).

Limitations (Sec 10): one corpus (Ubuntu IRC, technical support), one model, zero-shot, best run per setting, length fixed at 15. The authors say that claiming general capability from these results would be 'scientifically inaccurate'. The paper has no timing or latency dimension, no voice, and no AI participants: all participants are human IRC users.

How strongly this applies: it is a 2024 zero-shot study of Llama2-13b on human-only Ubuntu IRC. Jev runs a stronger model on a different question ('which ONE agent should answer, or none'), and the paper always gives the next speaker. So take the directions from it, not the numbers. Those directions match our design and point at specific gaps.

1. Give Jev the structure explicitly. Addressee reasoning came mostly from the who-talked-to-whom list, not the text. Text alone was the worst AR input everywhere: on U6, 0.289 versus 0.454 with structure. If Jev's prompt is only rendered transcript text, add a compact per-message line such as 'Prasiddha -> Friday', 'Friday -> Prasiddha (reply to msg 12)', 'Leo -> (room)'. Fill it from data we already store: mentions, thread and reply parents, triggerMessageId/agentHop, the opening-name rule, and DM-ness. This is cheap and was the strongest lever in the paper. Our deterministic rules (an opening name counts as a mention; an addressed message is not ambient) are exactly the structure that text-only models miss, so keep them deterministic rather than leaving them to the LLM.

2. Expect accuracy to fall in busy rooms. AR accuracy dropped as the speaker's number of distinct partners grew, and the structure advantage held only when they had talked to 1 or 2 people. In a room with several humans and several agents, plain messages from a person who has talked to many participants are exactly where Jev will be least reliable. Our confidence-0.7 silence default is the right shape. Consider extending it, or lowering confidence, when the sender's recent distinct-partner count is above 2. Log that count with each Jev decision so we can reproduce the paper's Figure 6 on our own data (accuracy and silence-correctness by degree bucket) instead of trusting macro accuracy, which the paper shows hides this.

3. 'None' is first-class. The paper's dummy [OTHER] option ('addressing someone not in the conversation') is the nearest thing to our 'none / a human' outcome. Make 'a human present' and 'nobody' explicit labelled choices in Jev's output space, not just the absence of an agent.

4. Prompt wording matters for this kind of task. AR shifted 5 to 11% relative across rewordings, versus about 1% for RS. So any edit to Jev's prompt needs a regression set run before it ships. The verbose, explicit prompt tended to win for addressee reasoning; do not trim Jev's prompt for tokens without re-measuring.

5. Summaries are a fallback, not a substitute. Replacing long history with a summary costs accuracy in simple rooms and only nearly ties in complex ones; speaker 'persona' descriptions were useless. For long voice calls or rooms, give the full recent addressing structure plus the last N raw messages, and use a summary only for older history.

6. It says nothing about the timing gap we already know (Jev decides at dispatch and cannot see a human answering seconds later). The paper's setting is static: the conversation is frozen and the next speaker is known. That supports fixing the gap structurally rather than by prompting: re-check the addressing structure (did a human just reply to the asker, or claim the floor in voice?) right before the agent posts or speaks, and drop or soften the reply if so.

summary: A short (5-page) workshop paper from Kyoto University. It introduces TEIDAN, a Japanese corpus of spontaneous, goal-free discussions among three people, filmed with one camera per face and recorded with one pin mic per person: 10 triads x 3 topics = 30 sessions. Five sessions (29:20 total, all on the 'alternative capital city' topic) were annotated for addressee. For each turn, the label says whether the next speaker was explicitly addressed (A/B/C) or not ('O' = no one in particular, anyone may take the turn). Only about 20% of turns (75/387) name an addressee. The authors gave GPT-4o a zero-shot prompt with the topic, participant IDs and the five preceding manually transcribed turns, and asked it to label the last utterance A/B/C/O. It scored 80.9% against a majority-class ('always O') chance of 80.6%, so it is close to useless at spotting addressed turns. It almost always answers O, and most of its errors are false negatives. Adding a crude automatic gaze feature (OpenFace 2.0, the speaker's majority gaze target in the turn's final second) to the prompt made it worse: 75.2%, below chance. On a related task, predicting who actually speaks next (A/B/C only, 50% chance), GPT-4o scored 46.0%, also below chance. The authors note that the addressee and the actual next speaker can differ because of interruptions. Their conclusion: LLMs struggle with addressing and turn-taking in many-party conversation and need better ways to use context and non-verbal cues. It is a small, preliminary benchmark: 5 sessions, one annotator for 4 of them, no agreement statistic, one model, one prompt, no reasoning or few-shot variants.
findings: S3/Table 1: explicit addressees are rare. 75 of 387 turns (~20%) are addressed and 312 are 'O'. 'O' dominates especially during opinion statements. The authors argue that a system that ignores addressee information 'may potentially interrupt the dialogue in 20% of turn-taking instances', even if it detects end-of-turn perfectly.

S3: labels were built from IPUs (inter-pausal units, stretches of speech between pauses) merged into turns, with backchannels removed so only one person holds the floor (minimal overlap allowed). Annotators used both text AND visual cues such as gaze. One session was annotated jointly by the authors to align on the labels; the other four were annotated by a single author. No inter-annotator agreement is reported.

S4 prompt (verbatim gist): 'infer who is addressed as the next speaker in the last utterance. Answer with one of A, B, C, or O ... O represents the case where no one is addressed, and anyone can take the turn next'. The prompt also carried 5 context turns plus the current one, the topic name and the participant IDs, from manual transcripts. It was zero-shot with no reasoning step.

S4/Table 2: GPT-4o output 'Addressed' was 9 correct / 14 incorrect; output 'O' was 304 correct / 60 incorrect. So of the 75 truly addressed turns it called O 60 times. Addressed recall is at most 9/75 = 12% (my computation) and addressed precision is 9/23 = 39%. The model is heavily biased toward 'no one addressed'.

S4 (1), Table 3: the success case is an explicit question naming the target ('What do you think, Ochi-san? Do you have any specific ideas?' -> C). Note the name appears at the END of the turn, not the start.

S4 (2), Table 4: a false negative. A says 'Tennoji?' and C answers 'Not Tennoji, but Namba, I think.' The gold addressee is A; GPT-4o said O. The cue was C looking at A, plus the fact that C was correcting A's short interjection. A short elliptical reply to whoever just interjected is addressed to that person, but the text alone hides it.

S4 (2), Table 5: a false negative. C asks 'I feel like in Nagoya, Sakae and Nagoya Station are slightly separated, aren't they?' The gold addressee is B, because B had been about to recommend Nagoya; GPT-4o said O. Addressing can follow from who owns a topic, which may sit outside the 5-turn window.

S5/Table 6: gaze was computed with OpenFace 2.0 at 30 Hz, using a heuristic that thresholds the gaze vector (|y| within 0.2, |x| outside -0.2..0.2) and takes the majority gaze in the final second of the turn (or O if no target passes 50%). The result was Addressed 12 correct / 36 incorrect and O 279 correct / 60 incorrect, i.e. 75.2%, below chance. It found 3 more true addressees but produced 22 more false alarms. A noisy non-verbal signal pasted into the prompt hurt overall.

S6: next-speaker prediction differs from addressee recognition. It labels who actually took the turn, so there is no O option (chance 50%, since one of the other two must speak). GPT-4o got 46.0%, below chance. The paper explicitly notes that addressee and actual next speaker can differ because of interruptions.

S7 conclusion: 'marginally above chance' on addressee recognition, 'below chance' on next-speaker prediction, and gaze did not help. Future work calls for better ways to use context (including gaze and other non-verbal cues) and for new models.

Limitations (my reading, not stated as such by the authors): Japanese only; humans only, with no AI participant in the room; triads, not larger groups; ~29 minutes of annotated data, all on one topic; one annotator for most sessions; accuracy is the headline metric despite an 80/20 class imbalance; the next-speaker sample size is not stated; there is no prompt ablation, few-shot, chain-of-thought or longer-context condition, so 'LLMs can't do this' is really 'zero-shot GPT-4o with a 5-turn window can't do this'.

forLightbulb: 1) The base rate supports silence by default, but it also means accuracy tells us nothing. In this human-only data about 80% of turns address no one, so 'always none' scores 80.6%. Any Jev eval must report recall and precision for 'agent X was addressed' separately from overall agreement, or a router that never answers will look excellent. 2) The paper documents exactly the failure we would expect from Jev's silence rules: a zero-shot LLM collapses to 'O/none' and misses most implicit addressing (12% recall). Our CONFIDENT_P = 0.7 gate on agent-authored and person-opened messages pushes further in that direction. That is acceptable for agent-to-agent chatter (the goal there is to stop loops), but the cost is real misses on implicit addressing. Measure it rather than assume it is free. 3) Our deterministic rule only catches a name at the OPENING of a message. The paper's one clear success (Table 3) has the vocative at the END ('What do you think, Ochi-san?'). Trailing and mid-sentence vocatives ('...right, Finance?') are cheap explicit cues worth covering deterministically instead of leaving them to Jev's confidence. 4) The misses are implicit addressing that text alone hides. In Table 4 a short elliptical correction goes back to whoever just interjected; in Table 5 a question is addressed to whoever owns the topic, set more than 5 turns earlier. For Jev this argues for (a) feeding the immediate reply chain (who asked the question this message answers, who spoke last) and (b) per-participant topic or commitment ownership ('Finance said it would look at Nagoya') into its context, rather than just the last N messages. 5) S6 confirms our known gap: the addressee is not the same as the actual next speaker, because people interrupt. A dispatch-time decision cannot know that a human answered first. That needs a post-dispatch check (re-read the room before posting or before speaking, and drop the reply if a human has already answered an addressed-to-anyone or addressed-to-that-human question). Better prompting at dispatch cannot fix it. 6) For Live voice: naively pasting a noisy non-verbal feature (their gaze ≈ our floor holder, who spoke last, or VAD-derived signals) into the LLM prompt made results worse (75.2%). Voice signals such as wake name, floor holder, barge-in and stop should drive deterministic gating outside the LLM, not become extra prompt text that Jev must weigh. 7) Caveats on transfer: the corpus is Japanese, human-only, three people and 29 minutes; the model is GPT-4o zero-shot. summary:
Khan, Kirstein, Ruas, Gipp (Göttingen), "Speak for Me: Giving LLMs the Situational Awareness to Participate in a Meeting", EMNLP 2026. The setting is ONE LLM delegate standing in for ONE absent human in a multi-party meeting. At every turn it chooses SILENT or SPEAK. If it speaks, it first commits to a single proposition z_t and only then writes the utterance.

The main finding is about the prompt-only baseline. A delegate that reads the raw transcript (even a 50-turn window) stays silent on 51.4% of the absent person's real chances to speak. It reacts to explicit name-calls but misses implicit handoffs, such as a group question that only this role can answer. It also treats "this topic was touched" as "this point was made".

CAPA (Collaborative Agent Predictive Architecture) runs a perceive-act-recalibrate loop over an explicit meeting state m_t. The paper lists six fields (§1); the §3.3 Perceiver description folds decisions and open questions into one, giving five: active topic, decisions, open questions, participant stances, prior coverage, and floor.
- **Perceiver:** updates m_t from each observed turn.
- **Controller:** applies a six-step rubric and asks three helpers for advice. The Curator ranks the delegate's candidate points. The Coverage evaluator decides whether each point is Fresh, ExpandOnOthers, Partial, Reinforce, Skip or Acknowledge. The Speaker Scorer ranks who should naturally speak next.
- **Generator:** phrases the chosen proposition in the user's style.
- **Predictor:** forecasts the next turn. The forecast is hidden from the Controller.
- **Two judges plus a Recalibrator:** after the real next turns are observed, the judges score the forecast and the action, and the Recalibrator patches m_t and issues guidance such as dial-up/dial-down pressure and a cooldown.

On 137 AMI meetings with GPT-4o, silence drops from 51.4% to 2.5%, loose recall doubles from 26.1 to 52.2, Decision F1 rises from 38.1 to 63.0, and hallucination stays at 0.6%. The failure mode shifts from omission to selection (45.3% uncredited attempts). Ablations show the explicit state, not a longer raw window, controls whether the delegate engages. Recalibration only refines what it says.

Caveats:
- Everything is offline causal replay of scripted 4-person AMI meetings, plus 10 ICSI meetings.
- There is one delegate, not several agents competing, so no who-among-agents routing is studied.
- The decision path takes 21 s mean and 36 s p95 with GPT-4o, so it is nowhere near voice-speed.
- The evaluation rewards speaking when the human actually spoke, so it is tuned toward participation.
findings: Problem setting (§3.1): a delegate stands in for an absent participant u*. At each turn it picks a_t ∈ {SILENT, SPEAK}. If it picks SPEAK it commits to a discrete proposition z_t before writing any text. The paper frames this as a POMDP-style belief/policy split (§2, §3.3), but nothing is learned: every module is a fixed-weight, schema-constrained LLM call.

Table 1 lists six desiderata. (i) Strict causality. (ii) Participant grounding. (iii) Pre-generation commitment. (iv) Abstention sensitivity: SILENT is a first-class action, and a missed opportunity is penalised the same as an inappropriate interruption. (v) Explicit state maintenance. (vi) State-directed correction: feedback updates the state, not just the output.

The baseline failure (§1, §5.1, Table 2) is that the transcript-only delegate is silent on 51.4% of opportunities. Its cue policy is 'bound to surface invitation': it fires on an explicit name-call and misses implicit handoffs. Its content policy 'conflates topical relevance with proposition-level coverage', so a valid point is suppressed because the topic was already touched. A Reflexion-style baseline (post-action procedural memory) barely moves silence, from 51.4 to 49.5.

§5.2 locates the bottleneck in the binary floor-taking decision, not in timing. CAPA intervenes in 97.5% of episodes against the baseline's 48.6%. When the baseline does get credit, its lead-time distribution looks like CAPA's. 93.8% of CAPA's 595 credited matches are anchor-aligned or come before the anchor, with a median of 1.0 turn early.

Floor taxonomy (Prompt J.3, Perceiver snapshot):
- Open_Floor: the default after a statement; low barrier to chime in.
- Open_Question_To_Group: low barrier for a relevant reply.
- Directed_Turn (to X): the floor belongs exclusively to X.
- Dyadic_Exchange (between X and Y): a rapid back-and-forth.
- Turn_Yielded_Back (to X): the floor returns after X's question has been answered.
Each utterance also carries intent_type and target_addressed.

Controller rules (Prompt J.4):
- Action space: Remain_Silent ('Default when speaking is socially inappropriate or strategically weak'), Respond_To_Explicit_Cue, Respond_To_Implicit_Cue, Chime_In.
- Step 1, identity mapping: 'Do NOT assume names refer to you without explicit alias mapping.'
- Step 3.2, Yield-After-Self: if the floor is open AND the last speaker is YOU, default to silent.
- Step 3.4: an explicit cue OVERRIDES cooldown.
- Restraint rules: (1) Ranking Gap Rule: if speaker_ranking[0] > delegate_score + 0.15, DEFER. (2) If best_viable_fit = LOW, DEFER. (3) Open-floor restraint: respond only if the delegate is in the top 2 with MEDIUM or better fit.

Speaker Scorer (Prompt J.5) runs only when there is NO explicit address. It ranks ALL participants, humans included, as candidates for the next turn. The order of checks:
- Cooldown veto: only the immediate last speaker is vetoed.
- Content gate: no fresh content means it cannot recommend Proceed.
- Topical engagement: Driver (3+ contributions) > Active > Passive > Silent.
- Expertise match breaks ties.
It outputs speak_or_silent_hint ∈ {Proceed, Deferral, Acknowledge} plus a confidence.

Coverage Evaluator (Prompt J.5) checks each candidate point against the state's key_points, the recent transcript, and the delegate's own earlier contributions. It assigns one treatment: Fresh, ExpandOnOthers ('Building on what X said'), Partial, Reinforce, Skip, or Acknowledge (someone else has already addressed it, so only a brief acknowledgement is allowed). The Controller drops anything marked Skip or Acknowledge, then prefers Fresh > ExpandOnOthers > Partial > Reinforce.

Curator scoring (Prompt J.5):
- Relevance = topic_fit×0.6 + flow_fit×0.4.
- Novelty is scored 1-10.
- The intent factor is 1.5 for a direct answer, 1.2 partial, 0.8 weak, 0.5 none.
- Composite = relevance×novelty×intent.
- High: composite ≥50 and relevance ≥7. Medium: 20-50. Low: <20.
Each candidate is also tagged with a topic level: MICRO (last 1-2 utterances), MESO (last 4-5) or MACRO. An urgency spectrum (URGENT_OPEN, SOFT_OPEN, NEUTRAL, RESOLVED) weights MICRO against MESO.

Recalibration (§3.3, J.7-J.10): a hidden Predictor forecasts the next turn's speaker, intent, topic and floor effect (TAKES, KEEPS, YIELDS or DIRECTED_TO). Once the actual turns t+1..t+k are seen:
- The Environment Judge scores the perception error.
- The Delegate Judge scores the action error, flagging intrusion (spoke when the floor was directed elsewhere, so decision appropriateness is capped at ≤0.45) and omission (silent on an explicit cue, capped at ≤0.35).
- The Feedback Coach emits contribution_pressure (dial-up or dial-down), a post-contribution cooldown, contribution_balance (under, balanced or over), and an error correction.

§6.1 / Table 8, state ablation: replacing m_t plus recalibration with a 50-turn raw window drops loose recall by 22.4 points and Decision F1 by 24.7, and raises redundancy from 0.0% to 10.7%. A longer raw window does not substitute for structured state. Raw window size N (10, 20 or 30) makes no difference once the state exists (Table 15).

§6.2 / Table 9, recalibration ablation: removing only the Recalibrator costs 3.9 points of loose recall and adds 4.6 points of uncredited attempts. Decision F1 does not move (66.2 vs 66.7). Recalibration tunes WHAT is said; the state governs WHETHER to speak.

§5.3 / Fig 4 breaks down the 504 uncredited attempts:
- Incomplete match: 40.5%.
- Different proposition: 26.6%.
- Safety/quality flag: 19.4%.
- Late match: 13.5%.
Off-topic rises '5.2% per episode' against a 48.9-point drop in not-attempted. The authors call this coverage-restraint trade-off an open design question.

§6.3 / Table 16, backbones:
- Decision F1 stays between 57.9 and 69.2 across GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Llama-3.3-70B and Qwen3.6-27B.
- Gemini is permissive: 70.9 loose recall but 18.0% off-topic and 5.6% hallucination.
- Qwen is conservative: 17.8% not-attempted, 0% hallucination.
- The authors' advice is to calibrate the printed cutoffs and restraint constants on held-out episodes per model, because model size alone does not set the operating point.

Appendix B.4 / Table 5, latency and cost with GPT-4o:
- The critical path (Controller, three helpers and the conditional Generator) takes 21.14 s mean and 36.49 s p95, including a 3 s throttle per call. Provider time alone is 11.12 s mean and 19.05 s p95.
- The full architecture costs $0.2090 per decision. The response path alone costs $0.1069.
- CAPA spoke on 37 of 110 decisions.
The paper does not address real-time race conditions; everything is turn-synchronous offline replay.

§4.3 evaluation protocol: units are participant-owned idea units. Each episode has a cue (the information boundary) and an anchor (the human's actual turn), with a k=5 window. Outcomes are Strict hit (Δ=0), Loose hit (0≤Δ≤k), Uncredited attempt, or Not attempted. A hit needs the same proposition AND must be neither hallucinated nor redundant. The LLM judges agree with humans at κ=0.71 over 150 idea units and 150 same-proposition pairs. Table 17: a larger k inflates loose recall but lowers Decision F1 (75.3 at k=3 down to 54.5 at k=9).

Limitations and ethics:
- Evaluated only on AMI scenario meetings, plus the ICSI probe (Table 13: silence 1.2%, loose recall 73.6, Decision F1 64.8, hallucination 1.8).
- Parliamentary and other rigid-turn corpora are excluded.
- The authors flag impersonation and 'plausible-deniability speech laundering' risks and require recurring consent from every participant before any live use.

Not covered by the paper:
- Several agents competing for one turn.
- Choosing which ONE responder speaks.
- Speech arriving asynchronously or overlapping.
- Barge-in, or a human answering while the agent is mid-decision.
- Voice latency budgets.
CAPA ranks humans in its speaker scorer but always acts on behalf of exactly one seat.

forLightbulb:
The paper is about a different problem from Jev's: one seat deciding whether to speak, not a router picking one agent out of many. Several of its mechanisms still carry over directly, and one of its warnings applies to our silence-by-default rule.

1. **Silence-by-default has a measured cost.** A prompt-only "should I speak?" judgment missed 51.4% of real chances. The misses were implicit handoffs: a question put to the group that only one role can answer (Fig 5/8, "Are LEDs beneath the buttons?"). Jev's 0.7-confidence silence rule (for messages that open with a person's name, and for agent-authored messages) will have the same blind spot. We should measure Jev's omission rate on implicit handoffs, not just false positives.

2. **The floor taxonomy fits our rules almost one-to-one, and it suggests what to add.**
   - **Directed_Turn(to X):** "the floor belongs exclusively to X". This matches our "opens with a person's name → silence".
   - **Dyadic_Exchange(X, Y):** two humans going back and forth. We have no rule for this; an agent should stay out even if no name opens the message.
   - **Turn_Yielded_Back(to X):** after someone answers X's question, the floor goes back to X. Agents should not pile on.
   - **Open_Question_To_Group:** low barrier for the best-fit agent. This is the case our "silence" heuristics risk suppressing.
   Asking Jev to output a floor_status label alongside its pick would make its decisions auditable, in the same way CAPA's "omission → selection" shift made its failures diagnosable.

3. **Coverage beats topic.** CAPA separates "the topic was touched" from "this proposition was made". Its Coverage evaluator's treatments map onto what an agent should do:
   - Skip: someone already said it.
   - Acknowledge: someone already addressed it, so only a brief nod at most.
   - ExpandOnOthers: "building on what X said".
   This is the right shape for our known gap, where a human answers seconds after dispatch. **The paper does not solve that race:** it runs in offline lockstep, and its decision path takes 21 s mean and 36 s p95. What it implies is a coverage re-check against the latest transcript just before an agent's reply is posted, resulting in Skip or Acknowledge. That is a pre-send gate in the agent turn (bridge/skill side), not a smarter dispatch-time Jev, and it costs one cheap call, not CAPA's nine.

4. **Rules worth copying cheaply:**
   - **Yield-After-Self:** if the floor is open and the last speaker is this agent, stay silent. We already get this partly from the hop cap and the source-agent skip.
   - **Explicit cue overrides cooldown.** This matches our rule that mentions always dispatch.
   - **Cooldown veto on the immediate last speaker only.**
   - **Ranking Gap Rule:** defer if a human's fit beats the best agent's by more than 0.15. Jev could rank the humans present as candidates for the next turn, and pick "none" when a human is the clearly expected next speaker. That is CAPA's mechanism for not stealing a human's turn.
   - **Identity mapping:** "do NOT assume a name refers to you without an explicit alias mapping." This is relevant to our rule that a message opening with an agent's name counts as a mention, given user-editable names that collide with human names.

5. **Structured state beats a longer raw window.** A rolling per-room state (open questions, decisions, who-covered-what, floor) fed to Jev would likely do more than raising its message history: in CAPA, a 50-turn raw window lost 24.7 points of Decision F1 and produced 10.7% redundancy. Only build this if Jev's errors turn out to be recognition errors; we don't have that data yet.

6. **Thresholds depend on the model.** Gemini over-speaks (18% off-topic) and Qwen under-speaks (17.8% silent). Jev's 0.7 cutoff should be re-tuned on a labelled replay set whenever its model changes.

7. **Voice.** Nothing in the paper addresses barge-in, wake name, queues or latency, and its 21-36 s decision path is unusable live. For Live voice, take the taxonomy and rules only, not the architecture.

8. **Evaluation is the reusable artifact.** Its episodes (cue → anchor within k turns, scored strict/loose/uncredited/not-attempted, with LLM judges at κ=0.71) are a ready template for a Jev regression set built from real room transcripts: did the right agent speak, at the right time, with a proposition nobody had already made?

Directed turn to a human. A writes: 'B, can you check the webhook config?' Expected: no agent dispatched, even though Engineering fits the topic. Then B replies 'done, it's on'. Expected: still no agent, because the floor is yielded back to A.

Expected: no agent (Dyadic_Exchange), unless the pattern changes or someone asks the group. Today this probably wakes Finance, which is a candidate regression to log.

Human answers after dispatch (the known gap). A asks a group question at t0, Jev dispatches Finance, and at t0+4s B posts the full answer. Expected with a pre-send coverage gate: Finance posts nothing, or at most a one-line acknowledgement that adds only uncovered aspects. Never a restatement of B's answer. Without the gate this reproduces the gap; capture both as before/after.

Partial coverage. B answers with half the facts, e.g. a price but no billing cycle. Expected: if the agent replies at all, it uses 'building on what B said' and adds only the missing part (ExpandOnOthers/Partial), with no repetition of B's figure.

Yield-After-Self. An agent's last message ends with a statement, not a question, and no human has spoken since. A scheduled or heartbeat post from the same agent must not trigger another reply by that agent. Assert source-agent skip plus the hop cap: zero further dispatches.
Explicit cue overrides cooldown. Finance just spoke (cooldown). A writes '@Finance one more thing, what's the runway?'. Expected: Finance is dispatched despite having just spoken.

Ranking gap: a human is the clear expected speaker. B has driven the database discussion (3+ messages, a Driver). A asks 'so which index do we drop?' with no name. Expected: Jev returns none, or only acts if the agent's fit exceeds B's by more than 0.15. Engineering should not take B's turn.

Name collision and identity mapping. A human teammate and an agent share a first name, e.g. the agent was renamed 'Sam' and a human is called Sam. A writes 'Sam, can you send the deck?'. Expected: resolve only by explicit alias or roster mapping. If ambiguous, err toward the human (no agent) or require an @mention, per 'do NOT assume names refer to you without explicit alias mapping'.

Agent-authored message raising an implicit group question. Engineering posts 'Need someone to confirm the Q3 budget before I ship.' Expected: Finance may be picked only at Jev confidence ≥0.7, and the reply is capped by AGENT_REPLY_CAP. Measure how often a true handoff like this is missed under the silence-by-default rule (the omission metric).

Voice: human barge-in during the floor-holder agent's turn. In Live, an agent is speaking; a human interrupts with the answer to the question the agent was addressing. Expected: the agent stops (barge-in), the queued agent is dropped if the interruption covered its point (coverage re-check), and nobody restates what the human said.

Model swap calibration. Run the same labelled replay set (cue → anchor, k=5) on Jev's current model and on any candidate replacement. Track omission (not attempted), intrusion (spoke on a Directed_Turn) and redundancy, and re-tune the 0.7 cutoff until intrusion and omission meet targets. The paper shows these trade off differently per model (Gemini vs Qwen).

summary: Eckhaus, Berger and Stanovsky (HUJI) build one LLM agent that plays online text Mafia with 6–11 humans and decides when to speak as well as what to say. The architecture (§2, Fig 2) has two LLM calls on the same model. A scheduler is polled at a high rate (Fig 1 shows a decision about every second; §4.1 calls this "high-rate sampling"). It sees the persona, the goals and rules, the current time, and the full timestamped chat history, and it can output only <wait> or <send>. If it outputs <send>, a generator writes one short message, and the agent waits a typing delay of about 1 word/second before posting. The scheduler prompt changes with the agent's own message rate: below 1/n (n = active participants) it gets a "make yourself heard" prompt, and above it a "let them have their turn" listening prompt. Evaluation is the LLMafia dataset: 33 games, 3593 messages, 93 humans, Llama3.1-8B in 21 games and Llama3.3-70B in 12. The agent matches humans on message count per day phase, on timing gaps (Fig 5, with lower variance) and on win rate (Fig 6). The 70B agent was identified by only 14.86% of players, against 14.92% for a random guess. Message content is still easy to tell apart: messages are longer (Table 3) and an LDA classifier separates them at F1 0.98–0.99 (Table 4). Being the most talkative player correlates with being voted out (Fig 7). The paper offers no ablation of the dynamic prompt, no comparison against a turn-based baseline, and covers only one agent among humans, never several agents.
findings: §2 Scheduler: a binary LLM decision, re-run periodically, over the persona, goals, current time and the timestamped history (footnote 2, App A.3). The decision is remade as each new message lands, not once at dispatch.

§2 Dynamic prompting (Fig 2, green box): the agent's message rate is compared with 1/n, where n = active participants. Below it, the talkative prompt is used ('Remember to make yourself heard…'). Above it, the listening prompt ('Pay attention to the number of messages you sent compared to others and let them have their turn too! … Check the speaker name in the last few messages'). This is a soft fair-share budget, and n shrinks as players are eliminated (Fig 4: survivors talk more).

§2 Generator: given the same context, it writes one short message. A typing delay proportional to length (about 1 word/s, after Dhakal et al. 2018) is added before posting. The paper does NOT re-run the scheduler after the delay, so a message can go out even if someone else answered during the typing window. This is the same blind spot as Jev's dispatch-time decision, only at seconds scale.

App A.2: the scheduler uses max_new_tokens 7 and repetition_penalty 0.9, a constrained token decision. The generator uses max_new_tokens 25, temperature 1.3, do_sample, repetition_penalty 1.25 and no_repeat_ngram_size 8.

App A.3: the scheduler prompt says 'choose to send a message only if your contribution to the discussion in the current time will be meaningful enough', which is a 'meaningful contribution' gate. The default is listening, phrased as 'wait for now and see what messages others will send'.
Table 2: messages per day phase: Human 4.23 (±3.11), 8B agent 4.28 (±2.50), 70B agent 2.95 (±1.21). The stronger model chose to be quieter.
Fig 5 (text): the time since anyone's last message and the time between one's own consecutive messages both 'closely mirror human behavior, but with slightly lower variance'.

Fig 7: a striking peak at normalized rank 1. The most talkative player is the one most likely to be voted out, so over-talking is socially punished.

The authors praise this as strategic. For an assistant it is a failure: a directly addressed question went unanswered.

forLightbulb: 1) The paper's main mechanism is the answer to Jev's known gap: decide continuously, not once. Its scheduler re-reads the latest chat about every second, so a human answering a question two seconds later naturally flips it to <wait>. A Lightbulb version needs no polling loop. Before an agent posts its reply (and ideally just before the turn starts), re-check the room: if a human message with seq > the trigger seq has arrived that answers or redirects the question, drop or shrink the reply. The cheapest form is a post-generation gate, which is the paper's own §7 idea of generating first and then letting the scheduler decide whether to send. Inputs: trigger message, candidate reply, messages since; output send or suppress. The paper itself skipped this re-check after its typing delay, so Lightbulb would be closing a hole the paper left open. 2) Fair-share pressure: a 1/n speaking budget adjusted by prompt is a cheap, proven way to keep an agent from dominating. Fig 7 shows over-talkers are penalized. Jev could take a per-room 'agent share of recent messages vs humans' signal and raise its confidence bar when agents already dominate the window. This complements AGENT_REPLY_CAP = 2. 3) Silence as the default and a 'meaningful enough' gate match our 0.7 silence rule. The stronger model was naturally quieter (2.95 vs 4.23 msgs), so capable models do not need to be pushed to talk. 4) Do NOT copy App A.4: their agent ignored direct address on purpose. Our rule that an opening name or @mention is a request must still win over any fair-share or listening pressure. 5) Brevity: agents wrote 1.6–2.7x more words than humans and were trivially distinguishable (F1 ≥ 0.98). In casual rooms and voice, keep agent turns short to fit in. 6) Voice: the paper is text only and has no barge-in or floor model, so it gives no evidence for Live's floor, queue, barge-in or stop rules beyond the general principle of re-evaluating at the moment you speak. 7) There is no multi-agent result, so it says nothing about two agents racing. Jev's pick-one remains the right fence.

summary: HUMA (Jacniacki and Carmona Serrat, Soofte Research) is ONE LLM facilitator taking part in a group chat of humans. It is not a router that chooses among several agents. Every platform event starts a three-stage workflow: Router (pick one of 20 conversational strategies, Keep Silent among them), Action Agent (carry out the strategy with send_message, send_reply or add_reaction, with simulated typing delay), then Reflection (one sentence of context carried into later runs). The key mechanism is that the workflow can be interrupted. A new event that arrives while the agent is "typing" restarts the workflow at the Router, and the agent's scratchpad and intended tool calls go with it, so it can drop or change a reply once the chat has moved on. The evaluation had 97 Prolific participants in 4-person role-play chats lasting about 10 minutes, each with one community manager (human or HUMA). Participants could not tell HUMA from a human (AI judged as human 44.6% of the time, humans 46.7%), and subjective ratings differed by |d| < 0.4. There are no ablations, no measure of router accuracy or speak/silence precision, and no multi-agent setting. The authors list "groups where human participants are a minority" as an open question.
findings: §3.2: the agent is event-driven, not message-driven. Six event types trigger the workflow: participant joins, message sent, reaction added, reaction removed, reply sent, and typing indicator activated. A human STARTING to type is itself an input to the router.

§3.2/§3.4.2 (this answers our known gap): the Router→Action→Reflection workflow 'can be interrupted mid-execution by incoming events, forcing the agent to reassess its intended actions while preserving its internal scratchpad.' Interrupts that arrive during LLM generation are queued until generation completes. Interrupts during simulated typing restart the workflow from the Router. The scratchpad and intended tool calls are included in the new context.

§3.4.2: a dedicated strategy, 'Continue Pending Action', lets the agent resume what was interrupted. Re-routing can therefore end in Keep Silent (someone else answered), Continue Pending (the reply is still relevant) or a different strategy.

§3.3: the Router decides both 'When' and 'What' by picking one of 20 predefined strategies inspired by MUCA's 3W framework (What/When/Who). The paper names 'Keep Silent', 'Go Deeper', 'Ask Question', 'Bridge Perspectives', 'Recall Message', 'Refocus to Goal', plus 'Directly Mentioned', 'Continue Pending' and 'Tell a Story'. Silence is an ordinary strategy that competes on score, not a fallback.

§3.3 scoring: for each strategy an LLM returns Appropriateness A ∈ [0,1] given the full history. Timeliness T_s = min(1, k/N), where k is how many steps ago the strategy was last used and N is the number of strategies. The strategy with the highest A + T wins. This penalises repeating a behaviour, so the agent does not dominate or loop.

§3.3 internal inconsistency: one passage exempts 'Keep Silent', 'Directly Mentioned', 'Continue Pending' and 'Tell a Story' from Timeliness (T = 1 always), while the next paragraph names only Keep Silent and Tell a Story. Either way, silence and answering a direct mention are never penalised for frequency.

§3.4.1: send_message and send_reply simulate a 50–100 WPM typing delay. 'During simulated typing the agent remains susceptible to interruptions.' The delay is the window in which the agent can be pre-empted, not just cosmetic.

§3.4.3: parallel tool calls are allowed (for example a message plus a reaction), but parallel send_message calls are forbidden. The second and later sends return an error, and the system prompt pushes the model toward sequential multi-turn sends. This is a hard rule of one message in flight at a time.
§3.4: the action agent has three tools. add_reaction is a lightweight acknowledgement that sits between silence and a full reply.

§3.5: after an UNINTERRUPTED action, the agent writes a one-sentence reflection that synthesises context and its own recent behaviour. It feeds later router runs and keeps the conversation arc coherent.

§3.1 names the multi-party problems: optional participation, asynchronous bursts (one thought split over several messages and interleaved by others), dynamic flow ('new messages may arrive, potentially invalidating current reasoning'), and diverse primitives (reactions, replies, typing indicators that signal intent).

§4.1: a between-subjects study with groups of 4 (1 community manager plus the Interested, Regular and Critic roles), a Leonardo AI community scenario, about 10 minutes of live chat, and identical facilitation instructions for human and AI managers.
§4.3: AI was detected at chance, with overlapping 95% Wilson confidence intervals in both conditions (Fig. 2).

§4.4/Table 1: all differences are small. Human managers scored slightly higher on effectiveness, social presence and engagement, and the two were level on human-likeness. In Fig. 4, 'Encouraged Participation' and 'Bridged Viewpoints' lean modestly toward the human managers.

§4.5: participants' folk cues (speed 34%, language 28%, empathy 23%, naturalness 19%) did not predict which manager was which. In §5 the authors hypothesise that realistic delays, visible typing and occasional Keep Silent remove the usual signs of automation, but they ran no ablation to test it.

§5.1/§6.1 limitations: one domain, short sessions, role-played personas, no long-horizon or harm measures, no per-agent timing signature. Open question: groups where humans are a minority and use in work settings. There is no evaluation of the router itself (no precision or recall of when it should speak).

forLightbulb:
1) The paper directly addresses our known gap (Jev decides at dispatch and cannot see a human answering seconds later). HUMA's answer is to make the decision revocable until the message is actually posted. Every new event in the room re-runs the router during the agent's composition window, and the agent's draft goes with it, so the router can choose Keep Silent or Continue Pending. For us, that means a pre-post re-check: before a run's reply is written to the room (or before TTS starts in Live), re-ask Jev with the messages that arrived after the trigger, including a human reply or a human typing indicator, plus the agent's draft, and allow a 'drop/keep/revise' outcome. We already have run abort and steer, so the cheap version is that a human message arriving in the same thread while an agent run is in flight triggers a re-route that can abort or steer the run. The decision belongs where the posting happens, not in every caller.

2) Treat a typing indicator as a router input. HUMA routes on 'typing indicator activated'. A short hold when a human (especially the one being asked) starts typing would cover the 'human answers seconds later' case without an LLM call.

3) Silence should be a scored option that is exempt from repetition penalties, with an explicit anti-domination term. HUMA's Timeliness penalty is per strategy for a single agent. The analogue for us is a recency penalty per AGENT (the agent who just spoke is less preferred for ambient room_event turns) and possibly per behaviour. It complements our 0.7 confidence floor and the 2-hop cap. Direct mention stays exempt, which matches our rule that a mention means the agent answers.

4) 'Continue Pending' maps to our voice queue and barge-in. When interrupted, keep the agent's intended utterance and let the next routing decide whether to resume, rephrase or drop it, rather than discarding it or replaying it blindly.

5) One send in flight per agent (§3.4.3) matches our per-room+agent FIFO. It supports never letting one agent fire several parallel posts in a turn.

6) Reactions as a low-cost acknowledgement. The router could choose 'react' instead of 'reply' for thanks or acknowledgement messages, which keeps chatter down.

7) Caveats: HUMA is one agent among humans, not several agents chosen by a router. It has no measure of routing accuracy and no ablation showing that interruption or delay matters. Its goal of passing as human (fake typing delay) runs against ours (our agents are openly agents), so take the interrupt window, not the deception. The authors flag 'groups where human participants are a minority' as unknown, and that describes our rooms.

summary:
Wei, Shuster, Szlam, Weston, Urbanek, Komeili (Meta AI / Cornell), "Multi-Party Chat: Conversational Agents in Group Settings with Humans and Models". The authors built MultiLIGHT: three-person, asynchronous, role-played chats set in the LIGHT fantasy world. Anyone can post at any time, nobody is blocked by turns, and the time of each message is recorded. The paper names two skills that models trained on two-party chat lack: (1) turn-taking, meaning deciding when to speak, and (2) coherence, meaning replies grounded in several other speakers while keeping one's own identity. It compares four designs (Table 2):
- Silence OR utterance: each agent independently either speaks or emits __SILENCE__.
- Speaker AND utterance: one model writes "Name: text" for the whole room.
- Speaker only: a next-speaker classifier or generator.
- Utterance only: given the speaker, write the reply.

Turn-taking was scored as next-speaker accuracy against a random baseline of 33.3%. Reply quality was scored by perplexity/F1 and by live human evaluations in which one crowdworker shares the room with two model-played characters.

Results:
- The per-agent silence approach barely beats random (best 36.5%; 35.8 in Table 3).
- A central next-speaker predictor reaches about 49–54% (BART-400M best at 54.4%). It rises to 85.0% when it can see the next message's text.
- Training on multi-party data greatly improves reply quality and cuts mistaken identity from 25.5% to 2.2% (Table 5).
- With humans in the loop, a trained turn-taking model did NOT measurably beat choosing the next speaker at random (Fig 2). The authors conclude that in open-ended chat, who speaks matters much less than whether the reply makes sense. They call for benchmarks where strict turn order matters.
findings: §1: The two named challenges are turn-taking ('Speaking out of turn or being silent when a response is expected negatively affects our assessment of a speaker') and coherence, which includes keeping each participant's identity distinct.

§3 / App A: Collection was real-time and asynchronous. 'players can send their message at any time and it will be shown to all the participants'; 'there is no blocking of users due to turns'; 'we record the relative time that each message was sent'. This is the setting closest to Lightbulb chat rooms. The timestamps were recorded, but no model in the paper uses them.

§4.1 Silence OR utterance: one independent decision per agent. The authors note this produces 'situations where multiple AI-controlled characters want to speak, or an impasse where none do'. Their evaluation fixes these with rules: 'breaking the tie using the most probable utterance, or waiting for humans to speak, with a certain time limit'.

§4.2 Speaker AND utterance: one model predicts the next speaker for the whole room. 'If the prediction is a human speaker (or any other agent that it is not in charge of), then the model will refrain from answering.' Predicting a human as the next speaker is the silence mechanism. This is the same shape as Jev returning 'none'.

§4.3 Speaker only: a classifier or LM that emits a name. They chose the LM form because it 'makes it easier to generalize to an arbitrary number of participants, dynamically determined by the set of names given in the prompt'.

§4.5: The recommended composition is to separate routing from generation: use a speaker model (or only the speaker half of a speaker+utterance model) for turns and a separate utterance model to write the reply. Lightbulb already has this split (Jev, then the agent).

§5.1.1 + App D / Fig 4: Per-agent silence fails. About 2/3 of training targets are __SILENCE__, so the model learns to always stay silent. Dropping silence examples ('silence drop out', SDO) moves it from always-silent to never-silent, with no useful middle. Next-speaker accuracy stays flat at ~0.33–0.37. The fallback heuristic (pick the agent with the highest perplexity on __SILENCE__) ends up deciding most turns. The authors' explanation: 'having multiple models, there is low probability for all three to generate the right prediction simultaneously'.

Table 3: Next-speaker accuracy from history alone is 35.8 (silence-or-utterance), 49.5 (speaker+utterance R2C2 2.7B), 49.2 (speaker-only R2C2), 49.6 (T5 700M), 54.4 (BART 400M). The smallest model was best. Given the actual next message's text as well: 82.2 / 68.9 / 85.0. Knowing what was said next makes 'who speaks' far easier. That is direct evidence that later context resolves most routing ambiguity.

Table 4 / §5.2: Two-party-trained models (BlenderBot 1/2/3, prompted OPT-175B, LIGHT SotA) do worse on multi-party chat. Multi-tasking on LIGHT + LIGHT Wild + MultiLIGHT ([LWM]) is best: MultiLIGHT PPL drops from 17.44 to 13.25. Cringe loss trained on wrong-order and wrong-speaker negatives (App E) did not help (15.28 PPL).
§5.2.3: The silence-OR-utterance model also produces noticeably worse replies than the other approaches (MultiLIGHT F1 11.37–12.08 vs ~15.9).

Table 5 (human eval, p<0.05 on every metric): the multi-party-trained utterance model vs LIGHT SotA. Mistaken identity 25.5% → 2.2%, consistent 28.1% → 55.8%, contradictory 8.8% → 4.9%, nonsensical 7.5% → 2.4%, overall rating 2.5 → 3.8.

§5.3 / Fig 2: A trained BART turn-taker vs a random next speaker gave no significant difference in human ratings. Estimated from the bars: 'out of turn' is about 4–6% in all four configurations, and overall-rating bars are about 53 / 78 (random + SotA / random + ours) vs about 48 / 75 (BART + SotA / BART + ours). The authors' reading: 'no matter who speaks next, if the utterance makes sense there is little if any harm to the flow of the conversation'. They add that some utterances in Fig 1 'can perhaps be reordered'.

§6 Conclusion: 'The flow control subtask, however, has much less contribution to the overall quality ... as measured by humans.' Their open question is when strict turn-taking matters, and they say that 'requires building further benchmarks'. They flag that their open-ended role-play does not require it.

App F, a limitation to note: the human-eval harness is not truly asynchronous. Each round, the turn model picks a speaker. If it picks the human, the system waits; otherwise it 'blocks the human from sending a message' while the bot writes. So the paper never tests a human answering while an agent is mid-turn, which is exactly Lightbulb's known gap. Sessions ended at 15 messages total.

App C: Baseline arithmetic. For a single agent, an always-silent policy scores 2/3 accuracy but F1 = 0, and a never-silent policy scores F1 = 1/2 and accuracy 1/3. Raw accuracy rewards silence, so silence-heavy routing must be scored by per-agent F1 or precision/recall, not accuracy.

Scope limits: three participants only, every participant is a role-played fantasy persona, no task goals, no voice. The 'room' never mixes several humans with several bots and a router that can pick 'nobody', which is the Lightbulb setting.
