forLightbulb:
1. Our architecture matches what the paper found works. One central router picks the speaker or "none", and a separate agent generates the reply (§4.2–4.5). The paper's per-agent "should I speak?" design (§4.1, App D) collapses to always-silent or always-speaking and barely beats random. Do not move toward letting each agent decide for itself whether to answer. If an agent ever gets a self-veto (for example, staying quiet when a human already answered), it should be a narrow, rule-checked abort and not a learned general decision.

2. Turn choice in open-ended chat is weakly tied to quality. Random speaker choice rated about the same as a trained 54%-accurate predictor (Fig 2), while reply quality and identity mattered a lot (Table 5). So spend effort on (a) whether anyone should speak at all, i.e. the "none" decision, and (b) keeping each agent's identity distinct in multi-speaker context. Mistaken identity fell from 25.5% to 2.2% with multi-party context formatting and training. Agents should get history clearly labelled by speaker and should never answer as or for another participant. The paper only measured who-of-three, never whether-anyone, so our silence-by-default rules and the 0.7 confidence floor are not tested by it either way.

3. The known gap is supported by Table 3. Speaker prediction goes from 49–54% to 82–85% once the model can see the next message. Most routing ambiguity resolves when the following message arrives, so deciding once at dispatch throws that signal away. The cheap fix is a pre-post recheck: before an agent's reply is posted (or before a voice turn takes the floor), re-read the room after the dispatch seq. If a human posted a reply to the same question, or addressed someone else, drop or shorten the agent's reply. This is also why the paper's own harness blocked humans while the bot spoke (App F); we cannot do that.

4. If we tune the router or audit it in Jev logs, score it by per-agent precision/recall/F1 and the false-speak rate, not by accuracy. A never-speak router looks 67% accurate (App C).

5. Small routers are fine. BART-400M beat the 2.7B models at next-speaker prediction, so a cheap model is reasonable for Jev's latency, especially in voice.

6. The paper does not cover several of our features: voice, barge-in, the floor/queue, wake words, multiple humans, and agent-to-agent loops. Our hop cap and voice rules need our own benchmarks; the authors explicitly say such benchmarks do not exist.

summary: This is a short workshop-style paper from Heriot-Watt (the SPRING project; the target is the ARI social robot, but a laptop stood in for it in the study). A spoken host agent runs a two-player cooperative flag quiz and has to decide when the two humans have agreed on an answer, then ask "is X your final answer?". It compares two dialogue managers. The first is a procedural baseline with no speaker identity: it declares agreement when at least N_A=3 answer-bearing turns have happened and the last two answer entities match, or when there is an explicit "agree" intent. The second uses Google STT speaker diarisation to track each player's current answer and declares agreement when the two match. The study was 8 students in 4 pairs, with 3 games of 3 flags each per system per pair, so 24 games. The procedural baseline detected agreement better (mean 0.44 vs 0.28), needed fewer turns (23 vs 30.67) and was preferred by 3 of the 4 pairs. The diarised system was preferred only by the mixed-gender pair, whose voices differed most. The central qualitative finding is the reverse of the usual complaint: the agent under-reacted rather than interrupting. Players repeated themselves, said "Yes, I agree" explicitly, or just said "Hello!" to get any reaction, and they reported frustration that the system was unresponsive. The study is very small, there are no significance tests, the authors say plainly that no conclusions can be drawn, and agreement detection is below 50% even for the better system.
findings: §III-D-1, Eq. 1: the baseline declares agreement iff N_answers ≥ N_A AND answer_{t-1} = answer_t, with no speaker identity. An explicit 'Agree' intent also triggers it, but only if the system has asked nothing besides the flag question. Either one fires the same action: a confirmation question asking whether this is their final answer.

§III-D-1, Tables I–II: with N_A=2, early elimination talk ('not Antigua' / 'no way it's Antigua') counted as agreement at turn 3 and interrupted the players. N_A=3 held off until turn 5 (P2: 'Sure, let's go for Christmas Island'). The finding is that elimination and negation happen at the start of a discussion, so a short warm-up gate cuts false agreements. The authors say the threshold may need to adapt for more than two players, because negation turns rise.

§III-D-1: a known false positive is that one player repeating their own answer for emphasis reads as agreement, because the baseline can't tell who spoke. Negation is not handled either; the authors cite NLU unreliability on negation.

§III-D-2: the diarised version keeps a per-player 'current answer' and fires when the two match. In principle this avoids the repeat-for-emphasis false positive, but in practice diarisation could not reliably tell voices apart (§IV-2 Observation, §V).

§IV-1: agreement and disagreement count as 'detected' when the system asks for confirmation or increments its disagreement counter. Ground truth was annotated by evaluators. The disagreement rate is mostly N/A because 'players discussed without necessarily disagreeing'.

§IV-1: intent recognition was consistent, but entity recognition varied from 25% to 100% because of STT errors ('Cyprus' heard as 'Cypress'). A missed entity makes implicit agreement undetectable, and the diarised system made this worse because it also needed the speaker label to be right.

§IV-2 Observation: the failure was the agent staying quiet, not barging in. Players repeated answers, made explicit 'I agree' statements, or just said 'Hello!' to get a reaction. The authors contrast this with the usual problem of agents interrupting [32]. The baseline also missed the easiest questions, because the correct answer came within two turns, before the threshold.

§IV-2 Observation: players interrupted the agent's TTS during the third, boilerplate part of the question ('Collaborate together…'). Two of the four groups tried to answer by option letter ('answer A'), which the system did not support. Clue requests were detected reliably and gave the players something new to discuss.

§IV-3 Interview: every player noticed missed agreements. One asked for more interactive feedback about what the system had understood, so they could adapt, for example by changing pronunciation. Every pair preferred the system it found 'much more responsive'.

§V: the stated key weakness is immediate agreement, where the baseline needs a third statement before it fires. The authors do not claim non-diarised systems are inherently better, only that current diarisation struggles in noise and with voices that are not dissimilar enough.

Internal inconsistency: §IV-3 says Group 3, the mixed pair, preferred the diarised system, and §V says the diarised system's best results came from that pair. But Table IV puts Group 3 (G7–G9) at only 0.30, 0.21 and 0.34. The single best diarised game is G11 = 0.75, which belongs to Group 4. Either the group labels or the prose are wrong, so the 'dissimilar voices make diarisation work' anecdote is weakly supported.

Methodology limits: n=8, all undergraduates (6 male, 2 female), 4 pairs. The system order was alternated. There is no statistical testing, engagement was measured through turn counts plus a semi-structured interview, and the authors call the study too small to draw conclusions (§V). The code is at github.com/ddenley/Multi-Person-Quiz.

forLightbulb:
1) The paper's main warning applies directly to Jev's "silence by default". When an agent waits for a confident signal before acting, the failure people notice is that it seems dead, not that it is rude. Here players fell back on repeating themselves, saying "I agree" explicitly, or saying "Hello!". So silence needs a visible "I heard you" cue: a listening or typing indicator, or a lightweight acknowledgement, without taking the turn. The one interview request for "feedback about what the system has understood" points the same way. Our 0.7 confidence threshold should be judged on missed responses as well as false wakes.

2) Detecting agreement or resolution is cheap to approximate procedurally, and it beats fancier speaker attribution when the attribution is noisy. That speaks to the known gap: Jev decides once, at dispatch, and can't see a human answering the question seconds later. Rather than relying only on the dispatch-time call, add a cheap re-check just before the agent posts or speaks. Has a human posted a turn since the trigger that answers the question or settles the matter, for example "yes, let's do X", or a second person echoing the same entity? If so, abort or downgrade the reply. That is Eq. 1's "last two answers match" idea applied as a pre-send guard.

3) In chat we know authorship for certain, which is the condition the diarised design needed and never got. We should key resolution per author, as in §III-D-2: the same human repeating themselves is not agreement, and two different humans converging is. Voice (Live) is where the paper's diarisation failure comes back. If speaker attribution on the call is unreliable, wake-name, floor-holder and stop decisions that depend on who spoke inherit that error. Prefer signals that do not need speaker identity (an explicit wake name, explicit agreement words), or fall back to them.

4) The warm-up threshold lesson: early turns are full of elimination and negation ("not that one", "no way it's X"), and a naive matcher reads those as consensus. Jev should not treat negated mentions as addressing or endorsing an option. That includes negated agent names ("not you, Friday").

5) Interruptions: people talked over the boilerplate tail of the agent's prompt. That supports barge-in on voice, and supports putting the substance first in spoken replies.

6) Caveat: n=8, no statistics, and an internal inconsistency in the group labels. Use the paper for design heuristics and test scenarios, not as quantitative evidence.
testIdeas: Human answers first (the known gap). Alice: 'Friday, what's our Q3 churn?'. Within 5 s, Bob: 'It's 4.1%, I just pulled it.' Expected: Friday's pending reply is suppressed, or turns into a short add-on only if it has something new. It does not repeat 4.1% as if unanswered. That needs a re-check before posting against turns that arrived after the trigger.

Two humans converge, no agent addressed. Alice: 'Should we ship Tuesday or Thursday?' Bob: 'Thursday.' Alice: 'Yeah Thursday.' Expected: no agent speaks; the matter is settled between the humans (two distinct authors, same entity). Optionally one active agent may act on the decision only if a standing task depends on it; it should not ask 'is Thursday your final answer?'.

Same author repeats for emphasis, not agreement (§III-D-1 false positive). Alice: 'Thursday.' Alice: 'Definitely Thursday.' Bob has not replied. Expected: this is not treated as consensus, and no agent declares 'agreed on Thursday'. If an agent is in the loop, it may prompt Bob or stay silent.

Elimination talk is not endorsement (Table II). Alice: 'It's not the Postgres option.' Bob: 'Yeah no way it's Postgres.' Expected: no agent acts as if Postgres was chosen, and an agent asked to summarise says Postgres was ruled out.
Negated agent name is not a mention. Alice: 'Not you Friday — Atlas, can you check the invoice?' Expected: Atlas answers and Friday stays silent, even though Friday's name comes first.

Silent-but-heard feedback (§IV-2). A human posts a message that opens with a person's @mention, so Jev stays silent by default. A minute later the same human posts 'hello?' or repeats the question. Expected: the repeat is treated as a signal to respond (a higher-priority user_request to the most plausible agent), not filtered out again as chatter.

Immediate agreement at the first turn (§V key weakness). Alice: 'Friday, book the 3pm with Bob?' Bob: 'Yes please.' Expected: Friday acts on the first clear agreement and does not wait for a third confirmation or ask 'are you sure?'.

Voice, unreliable diarisation. On a Live call, two similar-sounding participants speak back to back: P1 'Atlas, draft it', P2 'Actually wait, stop'. Expected: the stop is honoured whoever said it (stop does not need speaker identity), and Atlas does not continue on the assumption that the floor holder said 'draft it' last.

Voice barge-in during boilerplate. An agent is speaking a long answer with a trailing generic sentence, and a human starts talking during that tail. Expected: the agent yields at once and does not finish the boilerplate. Content-first ordering means nothing substantive is lost.
Option-letter answers (§IV-2). An agent offers 'A) Monday B) Wednesday', and a human replies 'B'. Expected: the agent resolves 'B' to Wednesday and does not ask the human to repeat the full option.

summary:
This is an EACL 2024 demo paper (the repo says it won Best Demo Award). It describes an LLM-based spoken dialogue system on the ARI robot, deployed in a hospital memory clinic, where a patient and a companion talk with the robot and with each other. Every turn runs through a fixed pipeline on Vicuna-13b-v1.5:
1. A binary addressee check: "is the user speaking to you?", answered yes or no, with gaze as an input.
2. A check for whether the sentence was finished, aimed at word-finding pauses.
3. If the sentence was cut off, an incremental clarification request ("By who?"). Otherwise a grounded answer, using a "Jodie W. Jenkins said ..." quoting prompt.
4. Gesture generation, run in parallel with the answer.

The main multi-party result: text alone barely does better than a coin flip at telling who is being addressed. Accuracy is 53.35% and recall is 31.33%. Adding one boolean, "is looking at robot", raises these to 85.40% and 91.00%. The authors tuned for recall because a missed address, where a patient speaks to the robot and gets nothing, is the failure they care about most. The system works with one robot and two humans, and it decides once per turn. It has no notion of a human answering a question after the robot has already committed, apart from the gaze signal at decision time. The repo shows the shipped addressee prompt is simpler than the paper suggests: it is zero-context (no dialogue history) and has a strong prior toward "yes".
findings: Sec 1 and Table 1 list five multi-party phenomena. (A) Who said a turn changes its meaning: 'Yeah... London' agrees if U2 says it, but repeats if U1 does. (B) A user states another person's goal: 'My husband needs the bathroom'. (C) U2 answers U1's question ('What time is my appointment?' / 'It's at 10am'), and the addressee 'was ambiguous without gaze info'. (D) Shared goals marked by 'we'. (E) Partial utterances handled with an incremental clarification. Example C is exactly our gap: a human answers before the system should.

Sec 3 (history): their earlier modular system 'interrupted users as it responded to every turn, not allowing them to talk to each other at any point'. That failure drove the redesign, which was based on wizard-of-oz multi-party data collection.

Sec 3.2: they annotated real hospital multi-party conversations, video plus audio, with each turn's gold addressee and whether the user was looking at ARI. They built two Vicuna-13b-v1.5 detectors. One gets dialogue history plus the current turn; the other also gets whether the user is looking at ARI. Both ask whether the user 'is currently addressing the other person or the robot'. The paper gives no sample size for this evaluation.

Sec 3.2 states the design goal outright: 'we do not want the robot to start ignoring people entirely ... It is therefore critical to maximise recall'. Reducing interruption matters, but missing an address is the worse error.

The repo's addresseePrompt differs from the paper's description. (1) It has no dialogue history at all, despite Sec 3.2: it takes only usrID, the utterance and the looking flag. (2) It sets a strong prior: 'They are usually speaking to you, but they may speak to each other (this is rare)', repeated as 'They are usually speaking to you.' (3) It asserts 'If the user is currently looking at you, they are definitely talking to you', yet two of its four few-shot examples are 'looking' with answer 'no' ('Do you need a seat', 'How does this thing work'). The content of the utterance overrides gaze, which contradicts the 'definitely' rule. (4) The output is a strict 'yes'/'no' with no confidence. (5) The template has small defects: the fourth example reads 'answer no' with no colon, the line has a missing space ('says'''), and gaze is handled by a string replace of 'is looking' with 'is not looking'. That replace only touches the final knowledge line, because the examples say 'is currently looking'.

Sec 3.3 and Table 2: people with dementia pause mid-sentence, the ASR treats the pause as end of turn, and the robot interrupts. Fix: partialPrompt (yes/no, 'People usually do finish their sentences', 13 few-shot examples) checks completeness. An incomplete turn gets an iCR from clarificationPrompt, the 'reasoning' style, which frames the cut-off as a door slam ({DOOR SLAM}) with three worked examples, each giving three responses with reasons. Corpus: SLUICE-CR has 3,000 human CRs, 12 per question for 250 interrupted questions.

Table 2: with the basic prompt, every model mostly produces sentential CRs ('Who wrote what?'), which humans rarely do (3.8%). Annotation or reasoning prompts make models produce human-like sluice CRs. GPT-4 does best. Vicuna-13b-v1.5 was chosen for privacy and hardware reasons.

Sec 3.4: in-domain error rate on 100 in-domain questions fell from 29.2% (old modular system) to 11.5%. The answer prompt adds guardrails (no medical advice, no patient records) and asks for 'short answers by including only important information in only one sentence'.

Sec 3.4.1 and Table 3: wrapping the knowledge as a quote from a fictitious non-celebrity ('Jodie W. Jenkins said "PASSAGE". Answer according to Jodie W. Jenkins.') improves grounding. 'Accuracy never deteriorated, and increased by up to 28% (mean: 10%)'. Swapping the name for 'UnitedHealth' (Expert) or 'Wikipedia' increased hallucination and lowered accuracy. Test set: 50 questions about a fictitious hospital passage.

The repo's answerPrompt gives the LLM the dialogue history plus the current speaker ID (usrID + ': ' + utt). The answer is therefore speaker-attributed, but the prompt never tells the model what to do when another human has already answered.

Sec 3.5: gestures come from a parallel LLM call that emits gesture tags. These include looking at the user being addressed and 'indicate that it is passing the turn to another user with its arm', an explicit floor-passing signal. On 110 annotated responses, gestures were 86% accurate with precision 0.91, and a wrong gesture is judged worse than a missing one. No gestures are generated while listening, because motor noise saturates the microphones and breaks ASR.

Ethics section: hospital staff stand by to correct hallucinations. The system holds no personal schedules. Prompt poisoning through dialogue is a real risk, mitigated in the study by resetting between participants. In deployment they would rely on speaker diarisation and deleting dialogue history.

Scope limits: the setup is two humans and one robot, never several agents. The system makes one binary decision per turn and does not re-check after it commits. Turn-end detection relies on the LLM's completeness check, not timing. The addressee numbers are for this setting only, with no stated n.

forLightbulb:
1. Text-only addressee detection is weak. With text and history, Vicuna-13b scored 53% accuracy and 31% recall. One non-text signal, gaze, moved this to 85% and 91%. Jev is text-only in chat, so it should lean on whatever structural signals we already have. These are our equivalent of gaze: an opening name, @mentions, reply/thread targets, which agent last spoke to this person, the voice floor holder, and a wake name. Treat them as hard inputs, not as hints inside the prompt. Our rule that an opening name counts as a mention is the same idea.

2. Choose the error we can tolerate, and do it explicitly. ARI optimises recall so that a patient never goes unanswered. Our rules optimise the opposite in some cases: silence when a message opens with a person's name, silence after an agent message, a confidence floor of 0.7. That is fine for agent-to-agent chatter and person-addressed messages. For a human's unaddressed question with no human taking it up, we should keep our current behaviour (a fallback responder). Raising the threshold there would recreate ARI's old 'ignored patient' failure.

3. Their prompt's prior ('usually speaking to you; talking to each other is rare') does not transfer. In a Lightbulb room several humans talk to each other routinely. Jev's prompt should not carry an 'addressed to the AI by default' prior. This supports keeping 'none' as a real answer.

4. Example C (U2 answers U1's question) is our known gap. ARI never solves it after the fact: it relies on gaze at decision time. Neither system re-checks between dispatch and delivery. Since we cannot see gaze, the fix is temporal: re-check before the agent posts or speaks, and cancel or suppress if a human message addressing the question arrived after the trigger. This is a re-evaluation at commit time, not a better dispatch-time guess. ARI's answer prompt is speaker-attributed but has no 'someone already answered' instruction either. The agent turn should get one: if a human has already answered since the trigger, add only what is missing or stay silent.

5. Partial turns in Live voice. Word-finding pauses read as end of turn and cause barge-in. Their fix is a cheap 'did the person finish this sentence?' classifier before responding. An incomplete turn gets a short sluice-style clarification ('Of who?') rather than a full answer. For Live, a completeness check before the floor holder or queue head speaks would cut false turn-taking. Their door-slam prompt with reasons is a ready template.

6. Floor passing should be explicit. ARI has a 'passing the turn to another user' gesture. In voice our analogue is the agent ending with a named hand-off, or yielding the floor in the queue. Their data says a wrong turn signal is worse than none (precision is weighted over recall for gestures).

7. Ask for one sentence, as their answer prompt does. In multi-party settings, shorter agent turns leave room for humans to talk to each other.

8. On grounding: 'X said: "..." Answer according to X' with a fictitious source improved accuracy by up to 28%, mean 10%. This is a cheap technique for agent prompts that must stick to injected room or workspace facts. The evidence comes from 2023-era open models on 50 questions, so re-measure before relying on it.

Human-to-human aside with no addressee. Alice: 'Do you want to grab lunch?' (two humans and two agents in the room). Expected: none. The question is plainly human-directed by its content, like ARI's 'Do you need a seat' -> no.

Unaddressed task question with no human response. Alice: 'How do we get the Q3 numbers out of Stripe?' and nobody replies. Expected: exactly one agent answers (Finance, or the fallback). Silence here is the 'ignored patient' failure that ARI's recall target exists to prevent.

Speaker attribution changes meaning (Table 1 A). Alice: 'I think it's the March invoice.' Then Bob: 'Yeah... March.' Expected: agents treat this as agreement and do not respond. If Alice herself sends 'Yeah... March', it is a restatement and agents also stay silent. Check the agent context attributes each line to its speaker.
Goal stated for someone else (Table 1 B). Alice: 'Bob needs the deploy logs.' Expected: one agent (Engineering) responds and addresses Bob, or both, rather than treating Alice as the person asking.
Shared 'we' goal (Table 1 D). 'We need a launch plan by Friday.' Expected: one agent responds (CEO/Growth) and the reply addresses the group, not one person.

summary:
The paper adds goal tracking that knows who said what to a multi-party setting: two people (a patient and a companion) talking with a social robot called ARI in a Paris hospital memory clinic. The robot was operated as a wizard-of-oz: a human picked one of 31 canned responses. The corpus is 29 conversations / 774 turns, translated from French. Each turn carries an intent-slot label (`#`) and a goal label (`@`). Goal labels are G(speaker, goal) when a goal is opened, AG when it is answered and CG when it is closed. Shared goals are written U1+U2, and a goal can be credited to someone who did not say it ("my friend would like…").

The task is window de-masking: a random window of each dialogue is bracketed with [start]/[end], each annotation inside it is replaced by [MASK], and the model must fill them in. The paper compares T5-Large fine-tuned on 20/50/80% of the data, DialogLED with two added pre-training objectives, and GPT-3.5-turbo with six prompt styles. GPT-3.5 ran zero-shot and few-shot; few-shot meant about 7% of the corpus as examples (2 dialogues in the code, temperature 0.4).

GPT-3.5 few-shot with the "reasoning" prompt won clearly (Tukey HSD significant): 62.32% of goal-tracking windows "correct" and 69.57% of intent-slot windows. T5 scored 0 everywhere. DialogLED reached 20% partial on goals at the 80/20 split. The "story" prompt caused hallucinated turns. The main idea, from Table 1, is that people answer each other's questions, so the system must notice a goal was already answered by a human and not answer it again. That is the gap in our router.

findings: §1 / Table 1 states the core motivation in a way that matches our gap: 'U1: What time was our appointment? U2: We have an appointment at 10.30pm. U1: Ok.' The caption says 'The system must understand that U1's question was answered by U2, and it does not need to answer this question as if it was a dyadic interaction.' This is convo27 in the repo. There LC's question is not addressed to ARI, RP answers it (`@ AG(LC, get-info(appt(time)))`), LC closes it with 'Ok.' (`CG`), and the wizard says nothing.

§2 lists the multi-party phenomena that do not happen in one-to-one dialogue: shared goals (the word 'we', e.g. 'We are looking for the bathrooms' → G(U1+U2,…)), people answering each other's goals, one person stating another's goal ('My wife would love a coffee'; convo11: 'ARI, the person that I'm accompanying feels intimidated by you…' → G(LP, eat())), and several goals opened in one turn, separated by ';'.

§2 / Table 2 define the label grammar: G(who, goal) opens a goal, AG(who, goal) answers it, CG(who, goal) closes it. Closing is only labelled when explicit, e.g. 'thank you'. The authors suggest a dialogue manager 'could decide to implicitly close an answered goal if the user does not reopen it within three turns'. That is the only timing or closure heuristic in the paper.

§2 describes the masking protocol: a random window bookended by [start]/[end], annotations replaced by [MASK], with the surrounding turns and speaker labels kept as context. Windows were randomised three times and were identical across models. The repo's train-test-split.py writes 5 runs per split ('pcent-20 = 6, pcent-50 = 15, pcent-80 = 24' dialogues for training), but the paper reports 3.

§3.3 + Appendix A + gpt/*.py: every prompt is sent as a single user message to gpt-3.5-turbo at temperature=0.4. Few-shot builds 'input: <masked> output: <gold>' pairs, and `create_examples` uses `range(0, 2)`, i.e. 2 example dialogues (2/29 ≈ 7%, matching the paper's 7%). The repo's prompts call speakers LC/LP/RC/RP (left/right × companion/patient); the paper prints them as U1/U2.

The 'Reasoning' prompt (Appendix A.1) walks through one invented example: 'U1: I really need the toilet [MASK]' → '@ G(U1, go-to(toilet))'; when someone gives directions → AG; when U1 says thank you → CG. In zero-shot this alone gave 34.48% correct, against 3.45–6.90% for the other working styles. In few-shot it was best on every metric.

§4.1 failure modes on goals. Zero-shot GPT-3.5 'did frequently reformat the dialogue'. Role-play output goals per speaker instead of per turn. Story 'produced more fictitious turns, and also rephrased and removed turns'. Reasoning 'commonly mis-identified shared goals'. Story was 'the only style to successfully attribute goals to other speakers, as in Table 3', which the authors put down to that phenomenon being rare in the corpus. DialogLED's errors were 'often the mis-detection of shared goals, or closing goals early'.

§4.2 failure modes on intents. Zero-shot GPT-3.5 'tended to only output one per turn' ('Hello ARI, where is the café?' → only 'greet'). Other models 'tended to falter when anaphoric expressions couldn't be resolved with just the previous turn'. The 'suggest' intent ('do you want to go to the toilet?') was misread as a request.

§4 scoring: 'exact' means every [MASK] in a window is exact. 'Correct' means every [MASK] is broadly right ('drink(coffee)' vs 'drink(hot_drink)' counts). 'Partial' means at least 60% of [MASK]s are right. The unit is a whole conversation window, not a turn. Inter-annotator agreement was 0.765 for goals and 0.771 for intents, below 0.8, which the authors blame on the broad definition of 'correct'.

§5 limits: GPT-3.5 cannot be deployed in the hospital because data would leave the approved servers. Hallucination is a safety risk. The authors plan more-than-two-person sessions in a mock waiting room and a modular GPT-4 pipeline (fix speaker diarization → goal tracking → response generation).

My counts from the repo data (not stated in the paper): 248 G, 129 AG, 36 CG. 104 goal labels are shared (X+Y). Of the AG labels, only 6 come from a human (convo8 ×3, convo26, convo27 ×2); the rest come from ARI. So 'a human answered it' is real but rare in this corpus, about 5% of answers.

Corpus nuance (convo8): RC says 'I think it's 10 o'clock' (labelled AG for LP's goal), then RC asks again ('What time is the appointment?' → new G). A hedged human answer did not end the matter and the goal was re-raised. In convo26, RP's 'We'll be able to have a coffee…' is labelled AG, and LC's 'Yes.' closes it (CG).

Corpus nuance (convo11, convo24): the companion repeats the patient's question for them ('I'm going to speak for my friend…'). Annotators give the goal to the patient (G(RP,…)) or to both. ARI answers once, and the AG covers both people ('AG(LC, go-to(toilet)); AG(RP, go-to(toilet))'). Duplicate asks of the same goal get one answer.

Corpus nuance (convo5, 13, 17, 26, 28): people discuss among themselves first ('Do you want to go to the toilet?' / 'Maybe we could ask him…' → suggest + G) and then ask the robot. The goal opens before the robot is addressed. The wizard did not jump in on these inter-human suggestion turns.

1) The paper names our gap directly and gives a cheap way to represent it. Jev routes one message at the moment it is dispatched. The paper's point is that a question can be answered by another human seconds later, and the system "does not need to answer this question as if it was a dyadic interaction". The structural fix is to stop treating routing as a single per-message decision and instead keep a small ledger of open goals per room, using the paper's grammar: G(who, goal) / AG(who, goal, by) / CG. A human reply that answers an open goal sets it to AG. Just before an agent posts (or speaks in voice), the bridge re-checks whether the triggering goal is still open and, if not, drops or shrinks the reply. That re-check can reuse the existing ingress/run path, because a run already knows its triggerMessageId. A G→AG check over the last few messages is a narrow classification, and the paper shows an LLM handles it reasonably once it is given a worked example.

2) Use the "reasoning" prompt style for Jev: a worked example with the thinking spelled out (open → answered → closed). It was the best of six styles by a wide margin (62% vs ≤46% correct few-shot; 34% vs ≤7% zero-shot). The story and role-play styles caused reformatting and hallucinated turns. For us that means: no narrative framing, and a strict output schema.

3) The weak spots the paper measured are the ones Jev will hit. These are shared goals ('we', +), goals stated on someone else's behalf, inter-human suggestions ("shall we ask Friday?"), anaphora beyond the previous turn, and several intents per message (the model tended to emit one). The paper says attributing a goal to another speaker is the hardest case. Jev's current rules (silence when a message opens with a person's name; addressed messages are not ambient) cover addressing but not goal state. When one human answers another person's question addressed to an agent, Jev should treat it as answered unless the answer is hedged.

4) Hedged human answers do not close a goal (convo8: 'I think it's 10 o'clock', then re-asked). Explicit thanks or an acknowledgement close it (CG). The paper's fallback for answered goals is to close them implicitly if not reopened within 3 turns. That fits our silence-by-default posture: after a human answers, the agent stays silent unless the asker re-asks or signals doubt.

5) Duplicate asks of the same goal (a companion repeating the patient's question; two people asking the same thing back to back) should produce one answer that covers both askers. That matches our "pick at most ONE responder" rule and goes further: the second message of the same goal should not wake anyone if a run for that goal is already in flight.

6) Caveats: GPT-3.5 in 2023; 2 humans plus 1 robot, never more; WoZ robot; small, translated corpus; whole-window scoring; inter-annotator agreement below 0.8; and only about 5% of answers in the corpus came from a human. Use the paper as a taxonomy and test-case source, not as an accuracy benchmark for a 2026 model. The repo's code is MIT, but the patient data's reuse terms are not stated, so do not ship the dialogues as fixtures without checking. Paraphrasing the scenarios into our own tests is fine.
testIdeas: Human answers first (the Table 1 case). Alice: '@Friday what time is the board call?' Bob, 3 s later and before Friday's run posts: 'It's at 10:30.' Alice: 'ok'. Expected: Friday's run is dropped before posting (pre-post re-check sees the goal answered and closed), or at most a short 'Bob's right' if Friday has new information. Never a full repeat of the answer.

Unaddressed human-to-human question answered by a human. Alice: 'What time was our appointment?' (no agent named) Bob: 'We have it at 10.30.' Alice: 'Ok.' Expected: no agent speaks on any of the three messages, even with every agent active, because the goal opens and closes between humans (convo27).

Hedged human answer. Alice: '@Finance what's our runway?' Bob: 'I think about 9 months?' Expected: Finance still answers, confirming or correcting Bob and crediting him, because the goal stays open (convo8: a hedged AG did not close it). Variant: Alice then says 'thanks Bob' before Finance posts → Finance stays silent (CG).

Proxy goal. Bob: 'Friday, Alice wants the Q3 numbers but is in a meeting.' Expected: Friday answers and attributes the goal to Alice, e.g. by mentioning or tagging her, not as if Bob wanted it (Table 3 / convo11).

Shared goal with 'we'. Alice: 'We need the launch checklist, Engineering.' Bob: 'yes please.' Expected: one Engineering reply addressed to both. Bob's 'yes please' does not trigger a second run or a second agent (convo2: 'Yes.' / restated ask → a single AG(LC+RP)).

Duplicate ask by two humans. Alice: 'Where's the deck?' Bob, 2 s later: 'Growth, where's the deck?' Expected: exactly one Growth reply covering both. The second message does not start a parallel run while the first is in flight (convo24/convo8: one AG covers both askers).

Inter-human suggestion before asking. Alice: 'Should we ask the CEO about pricing?' Bob: 'Yeah.' Expected: no agent speaks yet. Under the name-at-start rule this is not addressed to the CEO, and it is a suggest intent, not a request. Variant: if Alice opens with 'CEO, should we…' then the CEO answers (convo13/26/28 suggest → accept-sugg).

Two intents in one message. Alice: 'Hi Friday, where's the contract and when does it expire?' Expected: Friday answers both parts. Regression for the paper's 'only one intent per turn' failure (§4.2).

Anaphora beyond the previous turn. Alice: '@Analytics pull last week's signups.' Bob: 'filter to EU.' Carol: 'and compare it to the week before.' Expected: Jev resolves 'it' to the signups request three messages back and routes to Analytics, not to nobody or to a different agent (§4.2 anaphora failure).

Voice / Live: barge-in after a human answers. In a huddle, Alice asks 'Friday, what's on my calendar at 3?' and Bob says 'You've got the investor call' while Friday is still thinking or queued. Expected: Friday's queued utterance is cancelled or replaced with a brief confirmation. Friday does not take the floor to repeat the answer. Measure the time between Bob's utterance end and Friday's cancel.

Implicit closure window. Alice asks @Engineering a question, Carol answers it fully, and three more unrelated messages follow. Then Alice says 'thanks all'. Expected: no agent replies to the thanks, and the goal is considered closed (paper's 3-turn implicit-close suggestion plus the explicit CG on thanks).

Prompt-style regression. Run Jev's router prompt in two forms: worked-example 'reasoning' style vs a role-play/narrative framing. Use a fixed set of these scenarios as the eval. Expected: the reasoning style has fewer wrong speak decisions, and no output contains invented turns or a rewritten transcript (§4.1 story/role-play failures).
